lines: The bike chain needs one hundred tons of aluminum in six months, and the price jumps around. So it buys a futures contract: a promise to buy at two thousand five hundred dollars a ton, no matter what the price does.

If aluminum climbs to three thousand, the chain still pays two hundred fifty thousand dollars. If it falls to two thousand, it still pays two hundred fifty thousand. That's hedging: giving up the upside to remove the risk.
An option is different. A call option gives you the right, not the duty, to buy one hundred shares at thirty dollars, the strike price. You pay a two hundred dollar premium up front for that right.

If the stock rises to thirty six, you buy at thirty and gain six hundred dollars, minus the two hundred premium: four hundred dollars profit. If it stays at twenty eight, you walk away and lose only the premium.
Your break-even is the strike plus the premium per share: thirty plus two, or thirty two dollars. Below that, the call loses money.

A put option is the right to sell. Pay one hundred dollars for a put at twenty four, and if the stock crashes to fifteen, you can still sell at twenty four. Your loss stops at three hundred dollars. It works like insurance.
The same tool can protect you or burn you. Hedgers use derivatives to remove risk. Speculators use them to bet with less money, and leverage makes losses grow just as fast as gains.
